title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text: For this analysis, I use the Adult Income dataset, a census-based dataset containing demographic and employment information for individual adults. Each row in the dataset represents one person. I focus on whether average age differs between two workclass groups: individuals working in the private sector and individuals who are self-employed but not incorporated. The dataset used here contains more than 40,000 observations, and after filtering to these two workclass categories, the sample still includes a large number of individuals in both groups.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text: For this analysis, I use the Adult Income dataset, a census-based dataset containing demographic and employment information for individual adults. Each row in the dataset represents one person. I focus on whether average age differs between two workclass groups: individuals working in the private sector and individuals who are self-employed but not incorporated. The dataset used here contains more than 40,000 observations, and after filtering to these two workclass categories, the sample still includes a large number of individuals in both groups.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Data
The dataset used in this analysis comes from the UCI Machine Learning Repository
My research question is: Do individuals working in the private sector differ in average age from individuals who are self-employed but not incorporated?


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)
df <- read_csv("train.csv")
df_clean <- df %>%
  filter(workclass %in% c("Private", "Self-emp-not-inc"))

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Exploratory Comparison
Before conducting a formal hypothesis test, I first compare the age distributions of the two groups visually and numerically. The boxplot below shows the distribution of age for workers in the private sector and those who are self-employed but not incorporated.


Code
ggplot(df_clean, aes(x = workclass, y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Workclass",
    x = "Workclass",
    y = "Age (years)"
  )









The boxplot suggests that self-employed individuals tend to be older than those working in the private sector. The median age is clearly higher for the self-employed group, although there is still overlap between the two distributions. There are also several older outliers in both groups.
To compare the group means directly, I calculate the mean age for each group below.


Code
group_means <- df_clean %>%
  group_by(workclass) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_age = mean(age),
    n = n()
  )

group_means


# A tibble: 2 × 3
  workclass        mean_age     n
  <chr>               <dbl> <int>
1 Private              36.9 30587
2 Self-emp-not-inc     45.4  3464


The average age in the private sector is lower than the average age among self-employed individuals. This suggests a noticeable difference, but a hypothesis test is needed to determine whether that difference is statistically significant.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
To better understand the uncertainty around each group mean, I construct separate bootstrap confidence intervals for the mean age of each group.


Code
private_boot <- df_clean %>%
  filter(workclass == "Private") %>%
  specify(response = age) %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "mean")

self_boot <- df_clean %>%
  filter(workclass == "Self-emp-not-inc") %>%
  specify(response = age) %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "bootstrap") %>%
  calculate(stat = "mean")




Code
private_ci <- quantile(private_boot$stat, c(0.025, 0.975))
self_ci <- quantile(self_boot$stat, c(0.025, 0.975))

ci_summary <- tibble(
  workclass = c("Private", "Self-emp-not-inc"),
  mean_age = c(
    mean(df_clean$age[df_clean$workclass == "Private"]),
    mean(df_clean$age[df_clean$workclass == "Self-emp-not-inc"])
  ),
  lower = c(private_ci[1], self_ci[1]),
  upper = c(private_ci[2], self_ci[2])
)

ci_summary


# A tibble: 2 × 4
  workclass        mean_age lower upper
  <chr>               <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Private              36.9  36.7  37.0
2 Self-emp-not-inc     45.4  44.9  45.9


The table above gives the observed mean age for each group along with the lower and upper bounds of the 95% bootstrap confidence interval.


Code
ggplot(ci_summary, aes(x = workclass, y = mean_age)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Mean Age",
    x = "Workclass",
    y = "Mean Age",
    caption = "Source: Adult Income Dataset"
  )









The confidence intervals provide a visual summary of uncertainty around each mean. In this case, the intervals show that the self-employed group has a higher average age than the private-sector group. If the intervals do not overlap much, that is a strong visual clue that the groups differ.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Hypotheses
To formally test whether mean age differs between the two groups, I use a permutation test.
Let group 1 be Private and group 2 be Self-emp-not-inc.
The null hypothesis is:
H0:μPrivate−μSelf-emp-not-inc=0H0​:μPrivate​−μSelf-emp-not-inc​=0
This means that the average age is the same in both groups.
The alternative hypothesis is:
HA:μPrivate−μSelf-emp-not-inc≠0HA​:μPrivate​−μSelf-emp-not-inc​=0
This is a two-sided alternative because I want to test whether the two groups differ, without assuming in advance which one must be older.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Null Distribution and P-value
To test the null hypothesis, I generate a null distribution by permuting workclass labels and recalculating the difference in mean age many times.


Code
null_dist <- df_clean %>%
  specify(response = age, explanatory = workclass) %>%
  hypothesize(null = "independence") %>%
  generate(reps = 1000, type = "permute") %>%
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("Private", "Self-emp-not-inc"))

obs_stat <- df_clean %>%
  specify(response = age, explanatory = workclass) %>%
  calculate(stat = "diff in means", order = c("Private", "Self-emp-not-inc"))

obs_stat


Response: age (numeric)
Explanatory: workclass (factor)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
   stat
  <dbl>
1 -8.54


The observed statistic above is the difference in mean age between the private-sector group and the self-employed group. Because the order is Private - Self-emp-not-inc, a negative value means that private-sector workers are younger on average.


Code
p_value <- get_p_value(null_dist, obs_stat = obs_stat, direction = "two-sided")
p_value


# A tibble: 1 × 1
  p_value
    <dbl>
1       0


The p-value is essentially 0, which means that none of the 1,000 simulated differences under the null hypothesis were as extreme as the observed difference. In practice, this should be interpreted as p < 0.001, not as a literal probability of zero.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Visualizing the P-value
The plot below shows the null distribution of differences in mean age under the assumption that workclass and age are unrelated. The shaded region highlights simulated values at least as extreme as the observed difference.


Code
visualize(null_dist) +
  shade_p_value(obs_stat = obs_stat, direction = "two-sided") +
  labs(
    title = "Null Distribution of the Difference in Mean Age",
    x = "Difference in Means",
    y = "Count",
    caption = "Source: Adult Income Dataset"
  )









The null distribution is centered near 0, which is what we would expect if the two groups truly had the same average age. The observed difference falls far from the center of this distribution, and the shaded area is extremely small. This indicates that the observed difference would be very unlikely if the null hypothesis were true.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Decision
For this analysis, I use a significance level of α=0.05, which is a standard threshold in statistical testing.
Because the p-value is far below 0.05, I reject the null hypothesis. There is strong statistical evidence that average age differs between individuals working in the private sector and those who are self-employed but not incorporated.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Practical Significance
Statistical significance does not automatically mean the difference is important in practice, so it is useful to consider the size of the effect. In this dataset, the average age for private-sector workers is about 36.9 years, while the average age for self-employed workers is about 45.4 years. This is a difference of roughly 8.5 years, which is substantial in real-world terms.
This difference may reflect differences in career paths. Self-employment may be more common among older adults who have accumulated more work experience, resources, or professional independence over time. That means age differences between these groups may not be caused by workclass itself, but instead may reflect broader life-cycle and labor-market patterns.

title: Post 3: Hypothesis Test Comparing Mean Age Across Workclass Groups
text:
Conclusion
In this post, I examined whether average age differs between private-sector workers and self-employed workers in the Adult Income dataset. The exploratory boxplot, the group means, the bootstrap confidence intervals, and the permutation test all point to the same conclusion: self-employed individuals in this sample are older on average than private-sector workers. The p-value was extremely small, providing strong evidence against the null hypothesis of no difference. The observed gap of about 8.5 years is also practically meaningful, although the comparison should be interpreted carefully because these groups may differ in other ways beyond workclass alone.

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
This dataset comes from the World Bank and contains information on country populations. Each observation represents a country in a given year, and for this analysis I focus on data from 2022 to examine how population is distributed globally.
The data was accessed using the World Bank database through the WDI R package, which retrieves data directly from the World Bank API.
I am particularly interested in population as a foundational variable in my broader research on the gendered impacts of economic sanctions. Population size and distribution shape how sanctions affect different groups, including access to resources, labor markets, and social services. Understanding global population patterns provides important context for analyzing how economic and political pressures may be experienced differently across countries.
The data was accessed using the World Bank database through the WDI R package.

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
This dataset comes from the World Bank and contains information on country populations. Each observation represents a country in a given year, and for this analysis I focus on data from 2022 to examine how population is distributed globally.
The data was accessed using the World Bank database through the WDI R package, which retrieves data directly from the World Bank API.
I am particularly interested in population as a foundational variable in my broader research on the gendered impacts of economic sanctions. Population size and distribution shape how sanctions affect different groups, including access to resources, labor markets, and social services. Understanding global population patterns provides important context for analyzing how economic and political pressures may be experienced differently across countries.
The data was accessed using the World Bank database through the WDI R package.

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
Variables
The main variables used in this analysis are described below.








Variable
Type
Description




country
Categorical
Name of the country


year
Continuous
Year of observation


population
Continuous
Total population of the country


region
Categorical
World Bank region classification


income
Categorical
World Bank income classification


pop_group
Categorical
Population size group created for analysis

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
Data Cleaning

library(WDI)
library(tidyverse)


pop_data <- WDI(
  country = "all",
  indicator = "SP.POP.TOTL",
  start = 2010,
  end = 2022,
  extra = TRUE
)


pop_clean <- pop_data %>%
  filter(region != "Aggregates") %>%
  drop_na(SP.POP.TOTL) %>%
  rename(population = SP.POP.TOTL)


pop_2022 <- pop_clean %>%
  filter(year == 2022) %>%
  mutate(
    pop_group = case_when(
      population < 10000000 ~ "Small",
      population < 100000000 ~ "Medium",
      TRUE ~ "Large"
    )
  )

The dataset required several cleaning steps before analysis. First, I removed aggregate observations such as “World” and regional totals so that each row represented an individual country. I then removed missing values for population and renamed the population variable to make it easier to use in plots and discussion. Finally, I filtered the data to include only observations from 2022 and created a categorical variable called pop_group to classify countries as small, medium, or large by population size.

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
Population Distribution

ggplot(pop_2022, aes(x = population)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50000000) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Country Populations (2022)",
    x = "Population",
    y = "Number of Countries",
    caption = "Source: World Bank"
  )








The distribution of population is highly right-skewed, with most countries having relatively small populations and a few countries having extremely large populations. This means the population distribution is very uneven across countries.

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
Population Groups

ggplot(pop_2022, aes(x = pop_group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Countries by Population Group",
    x = "Population Group",
    y = "Count",
    caption = "Source: World Bank"
  )








Most countries fall into the small population category, while relatively few countries are classified as large. This reinforces the histogram by showing that very large populations are uncommon.

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
Comparing Population by Income Group

ggplot(pop_2022, aes(x = income, y = population)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Population by Income Group",
    x = "Income Group",
    y = "Population",
    caption = "Source: World Bank"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








This boxplot shows that population varies substantially within each income group. Some groups contain countries with much larger populations than others, and there are several outliers, showing that population size differs widely even among countries in the same income category.

title: Post 2: Exploratory Data Analysis: Global Population
text:
Conclusion
This exploratory analysis shows that country populations in 2022 are distributed very unevenly across the world, with most countries having relatively small populations and a small number of countries accounting for a large share of the global total. These differences highlight how structural characteristics, such as population size, vary widely across national contexts.
This variation is especially relevant to my broader research on the gendered impacts of economic sanctions. Population size and distribution may shape how sanctions are implemented and experienced, influencing factors such as labor markets, access to resources, and the capacity of social services. For example, in comparative cases such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Afghanistan, differences in population size and structure may interact with political and economic conditions to produce different policy outcomes.
In future work, I am interested in examining whether characteristics like population and gender-related indicators are associated with different types of sanctions regimes, such as comprehensive versus targeted sanctions. This would help to better understand whether and how structural country-level variables influence not only the effects of sanctions, but also how they are designed and applied.
